name: loguru
workload: Google Benchmark of one synchronous formatted log call per iteration (one INFO line with three integers, an int and a 128-char string) written to a log file, stderr output disabled, glog flushed in real time (FLAGS_logbufsecs=0); 1 to 24 threads; loguru v2.1.0 vs glog v0.6.0. glog numbers are in benchmark_glog.txt next to benchmark_loguru.txt in the same report directory.
claimed_speedup: Single thread: 2392 ns vs 4324 ns per call (iterations:2000 repeats:5 mean), 1.81x faster (derived from page data); min_time 3 s, 1 thread: 2357 ns vs 4378 ns, 1.86x (derived); 8 threads: 3434 vs 5357 ns, 1.56x (derived); 24 threads: 4264 vs 5932 ns, 1.39x (derived). Not uniformly faster: at 3 threads loguru 4383 ns vs glog 3734 ns (glog 1.17x faster, derived) and at 4 threads (min_time) 4029 vs 4196 ns (1.04x, derived). The project's own README claims 25%-75% faster than GLOG on a MacBook Pro (Clang), about the same on a Linux desktop (GCC) in unbuffered mode, and about twice as fast with ~100 ms buffered flushing.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (GCC) 14.2.1 20240910, glibc 2.40; build.sh passes -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON (CMake Release flags, not echoed in the report); -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra; Google Benchmark v1.8.3
hardware: Intel i7-10710U (12 threads), ThinkPad X1 Carbon 7th, Arch Linux kernel 6.11.9, frequency pinned to 3.2 GHz with scripts/set_cpu_freq.sh, 15659 MiB RAM (report dated 2025-02-21)
tradeoffs: Single loguru.hpp/loguru.cpp pair with no #includes in the header (README: about 10% faster compilation than including glog in a medium project). printf-style by default, optional streams (LOGURU_WITH_STREAMS) and fmtlib. In the independent run neither logger scales with thread count and the lead over glog shrinks or flips under contention. Public-domain dedication carries no patent grant.
caveats: Benchmark is a third-party logger shootout (MuggleWei/cc_log_benchmark), not the loguru author's. glog v0.6.0 is not the latest glog (the ng-log fork now exists) and loguru is v2.1.0 while the repo's latest commit bumps the version to 2.2.0. Output formats differ: glog uses a custom prefix function, loguru its default prefix with uptime and thread name, so per-line work is not identical. Time column for multithreaded runs is (sum of per-thread time / threads) / total calls, not single-call latency; the faster of the two libraries flips at 3 threads. Single laptop, one run per configuration, report has stddev only for the iterations rows. The shootout's own analysis singles out fmtlog, haclog, Nanolog and quill as the faster libraries; loguru is not among them. The project's own bench dirs (loguru_bench, glog_bench in the repo) are public but its README numbers give no CPU model, compiler version or glog version.

name: PEGTL (JSON grammar)
workload: JSON well-formedness validation of canada.json, citm_catalog.json and twitter.json (nativejson-benchmark data) read into one in-memory buffer; PEGTL contrib json::text grammar over pegtl::memory_input versus nlohmann::json::accept on the same buffer, measured with nanobench.
claimed_speedup: Mean validation time per file from the 11 per-run values on the page (derived from page data): canada.json PEGTL 3.65 ms vs nlohmann/json 20.20 ms (5.5x faster); citm_catalog.json 2.37 ms vs 6.60 ms (2.8x); twitter.json 1.41 ms vs 2.42 ms (1.7x). Same page shows PEGTL slower than rapidjson SAX (2.51, 1.44, 0.97 ms), lexy (2.29, 1.08, 0.75 ms) and glaze (1.16, 0.73, 0.32 ms).
tradeoffs: Zero-dependency header-only PEG parser combinator library (main branch needs C++20, 3.x and 4.x branches C++17); PEGTL's own README makes no speed claim and publishes no benchmark. The result is for the contrib JSON grammar only (no DOM built), so it says nothing about a parse-to-tree workload. Parse errors are raised as exceptions (the benchmark catches pegtl::parse_error).
caveats: The benchmark is written and run by the author of lexy, a competing parser library, and PEGTL is a comparison column, not the subject; no one claims PEGTL beats nlohmann/json, the figures are derived from a table where PEGTL is slower than rapidjson, glaze and lexy. Compiler, flags and build type are not stated on the page and the benchmark CMake fetches PEGTL main.zip and nlohmann/json develop.zip, so versions are unpinned (page last regenerated 2025-10-13 per file history). nlohmann::json::accept is an acceptor, not the library's fast path for parsing into a DOM. Single Apple M1 machine. PEGTL docs mention only an internal 5-10% gain of one rule at -O0 (Rules-and-Grammars.md), not a comparison against another library. The category guess 'filesystems-and-io' with stdio/fstream baselines does not fit: PEGTL's file inputs (mmap_input, read_input) have no published comparison against stdio or std::fstream.

name: Loki flex_string
baseline: std::string (std::basic_string) of an unstated standard library, inside Boost.Wave
workload: Boost.Wave (the Boost preprocessor library) with std::string replaced by flex_string, as reported to the author by Hartmut Kaizer; input unspecified ('depending on input').
claimed_speedup: 5-10% faster (Boost.Wave with flex_string dropped in, per doc/flex/flex_string.html; the same page states 'no performance comparison suite is available at this time')
stars_or_usage: 251 stars (GitHub mirror); SourceForge Loki 4.4/5 across 7 reviews
tradeoffs: Policy-based basic_string (storage policies: simple, allocator, vector, small-string optimisation, copy-on-write) that is a drop-in std::string replacement; storage policy choice (for example copy-on-write) changes thread-safety and iterator-invalidation behaviour relative to std::string. Loki code targets compilers of 2005 to 2013 (Gcc 3.4 to 4.1, MSVC 7.1 and 8.0 listed in README).
caveats: Anecdotal, second-hand number with no methodology, hardware, compiler or standard-library version, from the pre-C++11 era (CUJ articles 2001 and 2005). The project's other components have benchmark code but no published results: test/SmallObj/SmallObjBench.cpp compares Loki::SmallObject with new/delete, malloc and std::allocator (and optionally Boost.Pool) but results must be run locally, and a web snippet reports Loki::AssocVector slower than std::map on insert and lookup in a third-party run. Licence mixed: SourceForge lists MIT and SmallObj.h states MIT, but flex_string.h still carries the older Alexandrescu permission notice. Last GitHub commit 2013-08-06; SourceForge status Beta, last update 2013-08-06.
